# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
Sections 2–4 are useful. The record-based output and time-tracking corrections are what the Halden paper needed, and most of the arithmetic checks out:

- 95.1/0.8 → +18.9%
- 98.4/0.859 → +14.6%
- 95.4/0.861 → +10.8%
- Hours falls of 14.1% and 13.9% are correct.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 → −2.6%.

The problem is the final step. The evidence supports "the Halden gain is roughly half what was reported, and uncertain." The abstract and conclusion instead claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact." The comment never shows that, and the strongest evidence against it comes from a paper the comment itself cites.

## 1. The comment ignores the Varden case-processing result

The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature" but doesn't mention Varden's other stratum. Case-processing offices showed **+12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4)**, persisting at nine months. That estimate meets nearly every standard the comment recommends:

- randomised comparison
- record-based output
- actual hours from timesheets
- registered analysis

It also fails the novelty story in §6. Varden staff didn't choose the change, so "a change that staff chose, welcomed" doesn't apply. Yet Varden's gain is about the same size as the comment's own corrected Halden figure of 10.8%. Two very different designs converging on about 11–12% is evidence *for* a real effect in non-coverage work, not against it. Citing one Varden stratum as definitive while leaving out the other is selective use of evidence.

## 2. Attrition is said to be corrected, but it isn't

The abstract says "correcting the first three [problems], the gain falls … to 10.8%." The first three are attrition, the output measure and hours. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is never quantified:

- There is no intention-to-treat estimate.
- There are no bounds (e.g. Lee bounds, or worst-case imputation for the seven organisations that withdrew after starting).

Section 8 then counts attrition as a source of the overstatement without any number attached.

The attrition finding itself matters if it holds up. Halden's paper says the withdrawals happened in the preparation phase, while the microdata reportedly shows seven withdrew after the schedule began. That contradiction should be documented (withdrawal dates, release version) and put to the Halden authors for a response.

## 3. Table 2 compares different samples

The 23.4% → 10.8% comparison runs from all 61 organisations to a non-random 17. Part of the drop could come from the subset being different, not from the corrections. The Data note admits this, but the abstract presents the comparison as a like-for-like correction.

The fix is straightforward: compute all four specifications on the same 17 organisations. The key missing number is the as-reported gain within that 17. The corrected estimates also need confidence intervals. With n=17, the CI around 10.8% is probably wide.

## 4. The hours components don't add up

The logs are said to show +0.7 hours per remaining day plus 1.6 hours on the day off. Checking that against the reported totals:

- 4 × (≈8.06 + 0.7) + 1.6 ≈ **36.6 hours**, against a reported **34.6**.
- Working backwards, 34.6 − 1.6 = 33.0 hours over four days is about 8.25 per day. That is roughly +0.2 hours per day, not +0.7.

Either a component or the total is wrong. If the total is right, the comment's conclusion doesn't change. But the discrepancy should be resolved, since hours are central to the argument.

## 5. "Billable hours delivered" doesn't work as an output measure here

Using billable hours as output in a trial that cuts hours builds in a mechanical fall in output. In professional services, this alone could produce the gap between record-based and manager-reported indices. It would also push the manager-versus-records comparison in the comment's favour. The comment should show Table 1 with and without the billable-hours organisations.

More generally, records aren't automatically the "true" output. Managers may count things the records miss, such as quality or the value of work. The 19-of-23 pattern is suggestive, but "overstates" assumes the records are the right benchmark.

## 6. The novelty argument rests on the wrong variable, and could be tested directly

- **Wrong variable.** Energy is a wellbeing measure, not output. Nothing shows that output per hour followed the energy decline.
- **Arithmetic.** Energy fell 0.32 SD in three months, so linear extrapolation reaches zero around month 8.7, not "around month ten." Fitting a straight line through two points can't rule out a plateau either.
- **Testable with existing data.** Halden's output index was collected *monthly*, and the time-tracking logs cover the whole period. If novelty explained the gain, output per actual hour should fall from month 3 to month 6. The comment has the data to check this and doesn't. That's the most important missing analysis.
- **Burden of proof.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" doesn't support "entirely an artifact." Saying a gain is entirely artificial is itself a positive claim that needs evidence. Not yet showing durability is a different claim from showing the effect is artificial.

## 7. The Varden meetings analysis is misrepresented

- The comment says it was "selected for analysis after the results were known." Varden reports collecting the meeting data in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results. It was unregistered, but that doesn't make it post hoc in the sense implied.
- Case-processing isn't a "subgroup" picked after the fact. It was a pre-registered randomisation stratum.
- Varden didn't present meetings as an established mechanism. The authors said explicitly that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and they registered a confirmatory test. Telling readers it "should not be cited as a mechanism" argues against a claim Varden didn't make.

There is also a substantive point. If removing meetings drives the gain, that is a durable reallocation of time, not a measurement artifact or a novelty effect. Halden's own interviews point the same way: 47 of 58 managers mentioned cutting meetings. The comment dismisses the one mechanism that most directly contradicts its conclusion.

My earlier caution about the Varden meetings analysis still applies (r=0.71 across 7 offices, and no baseline). But "unconfirmed" is not the same as "should not be cited."

## 8. Smaller points

- **Revenue.** The abstract lists the revenue comparison as one of four problems that "account for most of the reported gain." Revenue doesn't enter the per-hour calculation at all. The point is valid, but it belongs in a separate category.
- **Retail.** The −11.2% figure is based on three organisations. Matching Varden's −11.4% is a coincidence of numbers, not corroboration. Varden's figure is a difference-in-differences against control in municipal counters; Halden's is a pre-post index in private retail.
- **Deflator.** CPI may not be the right deflator for B2B services or for non-profit grant income. It's fine as an approximation, but say so.
- **Scope.** The conclusion generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" as a class, from a re-analysis of one pilot.
- **Data note.** It's honest and correct ("our corrected estimates … describe those subsets"), but it contradicts the confidence of the abstract and conclusion. The headline claims should be brought in line with it.

## Overall

As a correction to Halden, the comment is valuable. It confirms with microdata several problems that were visible only in outline in the working paper, and the attrition finding is new and serious. As a general verdict on reduced hours, it goes too far.

A defensible conclusion would be roughly this: the Halden per-hour gain is overstated by about half; its durability is untested; coverage-bound work loses output. The best randomised evidence, Varden case-processing, shows a per-hour gain of similar size to the corrected Halden figure, and whether that gain persists is an open question.

I can draft a reply-style referee report, or a short synthesis table comparing what each of the three documents shows on output, hours, selection and durability.
